Kuvitus: Kansainvälinen avaruusasema ISS: Illustration: the International Space Station ISS orbits the Earth against black space. A long truss runs across the station, and at each end of it there are two pairs of large golden-brown solar panel wings. From the middle of the truss a chain of cylindrical living modules runs across it, and white radiator panels hang from the truss. At the bottom is the curved edge of the Earth: blue sea, green and brown land, white clouds and a thin blue atmosphere.
Kaavakuva, ei mittakaavassa: satelliitti: Diagram, not to scale: a satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit drawn with a dashed line. The satellite is at the highest point of the orbit. The blue velocity arrow v points to the right along the tangent of the orbit. The red arrow of the gravitational force F points towards the centre of the Earth, and beside it the orange arrow of the centripetal acceleration a n points in the same direction. A thin dashed line continues straight to the right: the satellite would move along it without gravity.
Kaavakuva, ei mittakaavassa: kappale läh: Diagram, not to scale: a body is launched horizontally from the same point above the Earth at three speeds. The paths have been calculated from the law of gravitation. At too low a speed the path curves more sharply than a circle and hits the Earth. At the circular-orbit speed the body goes round a circle that stays at the distance of the starting point. At a higher speed the path curves more gently, and the body moves farther away and returns to the starting point.
Kuvaaja mittakaavassa: ympyräradan ratan: Graph to scale: the orbital speed v of a circular orbit in kilometres per second as a function of the distance r, where r is the distance from the centre of the Earth in thousands of kilometres. The curve starts at the surface of the Earth, r is 6 371 km and v about 7.9 km/s, and decreases ever more gently: a satellite orbiting far away moves more slowly. The points marked on the curve are the ISS (r 6 790 km, v 7.65 km/s), a GPS satellite (r 26 560 km, v 3.87 km/s) and a geostationary satellite (r 42 164 km, v 3.07 km/s), calculated from real orbital periods.
Kaksi voimakuviota samassa mittakaavassa: Two free-body diagrams at the same scale. On the left an astronaut stands on a scale at the surface of the Earth, drawn as a rectangle: the gravitational force F (weight) points down from the centre and the support force N of the scale up from the bottom face, equally long, so the acceleration is zero. On the right the same astronaut on a space station: the only force is the gravitational force F, about 12 per cent shorter, there is no support force, and the orange acceleration arrow a beside the body points down towards the Earth. The station falls with the same acceleration, so the floor does not press on the astronaut.
Kaksi rataa, kumpikin omassa mittakaavas: Two orbits, each at its own scale, with the Sun at the focus of the orbit. On the left the orbit of the Earth: the smallest distance from the Sun is 147.1 million kilometres and the greatest 152.1 million kilometres. The orbit is drawn with a solid line and a dashed circle over it, and the two cannot be told apart. On the right the orbit of Halley's comet: the smallest distance is 88 million kilometres and the greatest about 5 250 million kilometres, a very elongated ellipse.
Mallivoimakuvio: satelliitti radan ylimm: Model free-body diagram: a satellite at the highest point of its orbit as a rectangle. The only force is the gravitational force F of the Earth, which starts from the centre of the rectangle and points down towards the centre of the Earth. Beside the body a thin blue velocity arrow v points horizontally along the tangent of the orbit and an orange acceleration arrow a n down towards the centre of the Earth. At the bottom of the picture an arrow shows the direction of the centre of the Earth.
